items.content_snippet: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports service-managed partition keys for On-Demand Standard and On-Demand Advantage streams, automatically distributing records across shards without requiring customers to specify partition keys to publish data. items.title: Amazon EMR on EKS now supports IPv6 Amazon EKS clusters
items.content_snippet: Today, AWS announces that Amazon EMR on EKS now supports running workloads on IPv6 Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters. Amazon EMR on EKS enables data platform and analytics teams to run open-source big data frameworks such as Apache Spark and Apache Flink on Amazon EKS. items.title: Physical AI's Next Bottleneck Is Finding the Right Video — Rafael Levi, Bright Data
items.content_snippet: AI without data is just a box." Rafael Levi of Bright Data points out that LLMs train on trillions of words, but robotics has only about a million videos of robots doing things. Paying people to record staged actions produces biased data, because nobody opens a door naturally when told to. Meanwhile, the web holds billions of hours of real people handling objects and real physics, with gravity, motion and cause and effect. The catch is noise. items.title: World Models Need Causality, Not Pretty Pixels — Christopher Manning, Moonlake AI
items.content_snippet: In 2007, Google already had a language model trained on 2 trillion tokens, the same order of magnitude as today's frontier models. Christopher Manning, Stanford professor, former director of the Stanford AI Lab and now at Moonlake AI, uses that as one stop in a tour of AI history. It runs from Dartmouth in 1956 and Shakey the robot to the rise of LLMs, and it ends at his argument for what comes next: embodied intelligence built on simulation. items.title: Robotics Has Been Stuck for 70 Years — Deepak Pathak, Skild AI
items.content_snippet: Show a robotics demo from 1957 next to one from today, and most people can't tell which is which. Deepak Pathak, co-founder and CEO of Skild AI and a professor at Carnegie Mellon, argues robotics stalled because it was treated as a hardware problem rather than a problem of building a general brain. Collecting robot data by teleoperation at one example a minute, he calculates, would take the entire US population more than a century to reach GPT-3 scale. items.title: From VLM/VLA's to Embodied Agents — Armen Aghajanyan, Perceptron AI
items.content_snippet: Feed a model one hour of video and roughly a million visual tokens go in, yet the loss lands on about two percent of them, since the only ground truth is a transcript or a few labeled frames. items.title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto
items.content_snippet: The newest frontier model scores about thirty percent on a data lab's benchmark of decisions from PDFs, and Adit Abraham has met people who worked on PDF processing before he was born. The format was built to print, not to be reasoned over, and humans encode meaning visually: merged cells, line charts, unreadable handwriting.
